analysis.one_liner: Sets disclosure rules and basic rights for rent-to-own contracts, while blocking states from treating them as credit.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 14 cosponsors split evenly between the parties, the bill never left the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Rent-to-own stores let people take home furniture, appliances, and electronics by paying weekly or monthly until they own the item — usually for far more than the store's cash price, and without any federal law treating the deal like credit. This bill would have required stores to clearly show the cash price, every payment, and the total cost to own; banned practices like wage assignments and unlimited late fees; and given customers a short window to catch up after a missed payment. But it also would have permanently kept rent-to-own deals outside credit laws and overwritten state rules that require stores to disclose an annual percentage rate.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 2.3 million households a year that enter rent-to-own agreements — mostly lower-income families without credit cards or savings — would get clearer upfront price information, guaranteed ownership after paying the stated total, reinstatement rights after a missed payment, and a ban on confessions of judgment, wage assignments, and unlimited late fees.

how_it_helps.text: Merchants would have to disclose, before signing and at the display shelf, the cash price of the item, every periodic payment, the number of payments, and the total cost to acquire ownership.

Contracts could not contain confessions of judgment, negotiable instruments, wage assignments, waivers of legal claims, or clauses letting the merchant enter a home without consent or cause a breach of the peace during repossession, and no more than one late fee per missed payment.

Customers who miss a payment could reinstate the agreement within 3 business days (weekly payers) or 7 business days (monthly payers) without losing their ownership rights, and ownership transfers automatically once the disclosed total cost is paid, with no extra fees.
Violations would be enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission as unfair or deceptive practices.

analysis.who_pays: Rent-to-own companies would bear the cost of new disclosures and contract rules. Consumers in states with stronger laws would give something up too: state rules requiring an annual percentage rate disclosure, and state laws treating rent-to-own as credit, would be superseded.
analysis.who_pays_short: Rent-to-own stores; consumers in strong-law states

drawbacks.text: The bill would supersede any state law that requires disclosure of a percentage rate calculation, including an annual percentage rate, so the single clearest measure of how expensive rent-to-own is — which can run to several times the cash price — would never have to be shown.

It would shield rent-to-own agreements from the Truth in Lending Act and from state laws treating them as credit sales, loans, or installment sales, locking in the industry's status as a non-credit business nationwide.

The reinstatement window after a missed payment is short — 3 business days for weekly payers, 7 for monthly — and the bill's own findings frame the industry as simply 'meeting the demands of many consumers' rather than as an expensive form of financing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers in states with no rent-to-own law, the disclosure and contract rules are a real gain over nothing. But the price of those national minimums is a ceiling: by wiping out state annual-percentage-rate disclosure and state treatment of rent-to-own as credit, the bill would have replaced stronger local rules with weaker federal ones in many states. A consumer would see the total dollar cost but not the annualized rate that makes comparison shopping meaningful.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Tester introduced the bill on June 20, 2013, joined by Senator Jerry Moran; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
Fourteen senators cosponsored the bill, seven Republicans and seven Democrats.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing passed, so states kept their own rent-to-own rules — including annual-rate disclosure where it exists — and rent-to-own companies avoided the bill's new federal duties but also got no federal preemption shield. Consumers in states without any rent-to-own law got nothing new either; the outcome was the status quo for everyone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: strong-law states kept their rules

sides.party_line_note: The 14 cosponsors split exactly evenly — 7 Republicans and 7 Democrats — but the bill never reached a recorded vote in committee or on the floor.

industries.note: The bill would impose new disclosure and contract duties on the industry, but it would also permanently define rent-to-own as something other than credit and supersede state laws requiring annual-rate disclosure — locking in the industry's legal footing nationwide while customers still pay a total cost that can be several times the cash price. The industry's core interest in this bill runs against full price transparency for its customers.
States that require annual-percentage-rate disclosure or treat rent-to-own as consumer credit would have had those rules preempted, removing their strongest consumer protections.
